query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

cited_evidence.text: The development of Pt-based catalysts for use in fuel cells that meet performance targets of high activity, maximized stability, and low cost remains a huge challenge. Herein, we report a nitrogen (N)-doped high-entropy alloy (HEA) electrocatalyst that consists of a Pt-rich shell and a N-doped PtCoFeNiCu core on a carbon support (denoted as N–Pt/HEA/C). The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst showed a high mass activity of 1.34 A mgPt–1 at 0.9 V for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in rotating disk electrode (RDE) testing, which substantially outperformed commercial Pt/C and most of the other binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst also demonstrated excellent stability in both RDE and membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing. Using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements and theoretical calculations, we revealed that the enhanced ORR activity of N–Pt/HEA/C originated from the optimized adsorption energy of intermediates, resulting in the tailored electronic structure formed upon N-doping. In this study, we have synthesized an N-doped HEA electrocatalyst with a Pt-rich skin supported on Vulcan XC-72 carbon (denoted as N–Pt/HEA/C). The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst exhibited high long-term durability that it only lost 20.9% mass activity (MA) after 30,000 cycles and retained prominent ORR activity, with MA of 1.34 A mgPt–1 and specific activity (SA) of 1.93 mA cm–2 at 0.9 V, which are 7.4 and 6.2 times higher than those of the commercial Pt/C catalyst, respectively. Moreover, the membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing of N–Pt/HEA/C showed excellent durability for HDV applications, with a high current density (1437 mA cm–2) at 0.7 V and only 18 mV drop at 0.8 A cm–2 after 30,000 voltage cycles. The in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) coupled with density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the enhanced performance was due to the synergistic effects of the high entropy, multiple M–N bonds, and Pt-rich shell.

Recently, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted increasing attention in diverse fields due to their inherent properties, including high thermal stability, strong mechanical strength, excellent corrosion resistance, and fine trade-off effect on performance. As promising catalysts in heterogeneous catalysis, HEAs generally consist of five or more metals, which display the structure-dependent synergistic effects and enhanced catalytic performance in terms of activity and durability,. Moreover, since the HEAs can largely decrease the usage of noble metals and thus reduce the cost of catalyst, they have been attracted increasing research interests. For instance, Li et al. reported a small HEAs Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 nanoparticles (NPs) with a mean size of ~3.4 nm as an efficient catalyst for alkaline methanol oxidation reaction, on which the synergistic effects facilitate the site-to-site electron transfer during both reduction and oxidation processes. Cui et al. demonstrated that the synergistic effects between different metals in CrMnFeCoNi HEA sulfide can regulate the electronic states and thus enhances the oxygen evolution reaction activity. It is difficult to detect short‐range ordered nanocrystals using X‐ray diffraction (XRD) due to the limitation of the X‐ray coherence length.[ ,  ] Electron diffraction has a poor resolution for determining the precise d‐spacing. Thus, it is difficult to distinguish different kinds of oxide in an HEO sample based on electron diffraction patterns.[  ] X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) probes only the outermost surface chemistry, not the bulk properties, of electrodes. Therefore, limited information can be obtained. Moreover, ex situ analyses usually face contamination problems; air and moisture exposure can affect experimental results, especially for highly lithiated electrodes with strong reactivity.[ , ,  ] These problems may explain the inconsistent redox reaction mechanisms reported in the literature. Operando analysis is thus required to probe the electrode material variation during charging/discharging in real time. Operando X‐ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) is sensitive to the local environments and electronic structures of absorbing atoms, making it suitable for mechanistic investigations.
